speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I am Dr. Agent. You are presenting with double vision, difficulty climbing stairs, and upper limb weakness; let's start by asking when exactly these symptoms first appeared and if they fluctuate in intensity throughout the day.

speaker: Patient
text: The double vision usually happens when I look up or down, and the weakness in my arms and legs gets worse after activity but improves if I rest. I have not noticed balance problems or numbness.

speaker: Doctor
text: That pattern of worsening symptoms with activity and improving with rest, combined with diplopia on vertical gaze, is highly suggestive of a neuromuscular junction disorder. REQUEST TEST: Acetylcholine_receptor_antibodies. Do you have any history of drooping eyelids (ptosis) or difficulty swallowing?

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Acetylcholine_Receptor_Antibodies: Present (elevated); Neurological_Examination: Presence of ptosis (drooping of the right upper eyelid) that worsens with sustained upward gaze; Vital_Signs: Temperature 36.6°C (97.9°F), Blood_Pressure 125/80 mmHg, Heart_Rate 72 bpm, Respiratory_Rate 16 breaths/min.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Myasthenia Gravis.

The elevated acetylcholine receptor antibodies, combined with your history of fluctuating weakness, ptosis, and diplopia that worsens with activity, confirm this diagnosis. Since you have difficulty climbing stairs and upper limb weakness, I need to assess your respiratory function to ensure your breathing muscles are strong enough. REQUEST TEST: Forced_Vital_Capacity and Request Images of your lungs and chest.
